'''''Passiflora suberosa''''' is a species of [[passionflower]] that is native to the [[Americas]].<ref name="GRIN"/> It is commonly known as '''corkystem passionflower''' due to the corkiness of older stems. Other common names include '''corky passion vine''',  '''cork-bark passion flower''', '''corkstem passionflower''' and '''corky passionfruit'''.<ref>[https://weeds.brisbane.qld.gov.au/weeds/corky-passion-vine corky passion vine Passiflora suberosa] [[Brisbane City Council]] Weed Identification Tool</ref> In [[Latin America]] it is called '''Meloncillo'''. It is possibly also [[Cryptic species|cryptic]] and have multiple species in one.<ref name="Cryptic">{{cite web |title=Passiflora suberosa L. |url=http://tropical.theferns.info/viewtropical.php?id=Passiflora+suberosa |website=Useful Tropical Plants |access-date=3 July 2021}}</ref>

==Description==
===Leaves and stems===
[[File:Passiflora_suberosa.jpg|thumb|220px|left|Leaves of plant]]
[[File:Passiflora suberosa flower.jpg|thumb|220px|left|Flower]]
[[File:Passiflora suberosa (fruit).jpg|thumb|220px|left|Fruit]]
It is a creeping or climbing perennial [[liana]] up to 6 meters long. It has suberous stems in its lower part, glabrous to puberulent.

The leaves are simple, alternate, entire to three-lobed, with both sides glabrous, shiny green. They are 4 to 12 centimeters long when elliptical and up to 5 cm long and 7 cm wide when deeply lobed, sharp lobes, base rounded to truncated, glabrous to puberulent; [[petiole (botany)|petioles]] 0.5–4 cm long, with a pair of conspicuous and stipitate glands in upper half; linear [[stipules]].

The plant is known for the fact that the leaves on one and the same plant vary greatly in shape and size.<ref>{{ cite journal | last= Zona Ph.D.| first=Scott | date= n.d. | title= Shape Shifters | journal= Fairchild Tropical Garden- Garden View | volume= 57 | issue= 4 | page= Photo and caption p. 17 }}</ref> Another well-known phenomenon is that the lower part of the [[Trunk (botany)|trunk]] becomes corky with aging.

===Flowers and fruit===
The melliferous flowers are solitary or in pairs, and grow in the [[leaf axil]]s. Greenish or yellowish in color, they have 5 [[lanceolate]] sepals, but no petals. Flowering takes place from late summer to late winter.

The inedible fruit is not hardy and transitions from green to [[indigo]], purple and, lastly, black as it [[Ripening|ripe]]ns. The glabrous fruits contain a multitude of tiny seeds in a dark blue pulp, which are dispersed by birds.

<ref>Hernández & N. García. 2006. Passion flowers (Passifloraceae family). Red Book Pl. Colombia 3: 3: 583–653.</ref> (Not able to verify original reference(6). Forms .org/.edu reference this particular fruit as edible for people but may not have the best of flavor depending on ripeness.)

==Range==
Its range stretches from [[Florida]] and the Lower [[Rio Grande Valley (Texas)|Rio Grande Valley]] of [[Texas]] in the United States<ref name="NABA">{{cite web |url=http://www.nababutterfly.com/Passiflora_suberosa.html |title=Corkystem Passionflower - ''Passiflora suberosa'' |publisher=North American Butterfly Association |access-date=2010-08-22}}</ref> south through Mexico, [[Central America]], and the [[Caribbean]] to [[South America]].<ref name="GRIN"/> In 1909, it was introduced in [[Polynesia]] and [[Australia]].

It is extremely prolific (up to 1000 seeds per square meter), [[invasive species|smothering]] any vegetation it grows on, including trees. In New Caledonia, it is prohibited to introduce the species into the wild.<ref>Invasive species group, Invasive plants for the natural environments of New Caledonia, Nouméa, Agency for the prevention and compensation of agricultural or natural disasters (APICAN), January 2012, 222  p., pp. 126-127</ref>

==Reproduction==
Many clones of the plant are [[self-pollinating]]. In winter, the plant is [[plant hardiness|hardy]] down to temperatures around 7 °C. It can be propagated by [[sowing]] or [[cuttings (plant)|cuttings]].

This species is a host plant for the [[caterpillar]]s of the Gulf fritillary (''[[Agraulis vanillae]]''), Julia heliconian (''[[Dryas iulia]]''), Mexican silverspot (''[[Dione moneta]]''), red postman (''[[Heliconius erato]]''), and zebra heliconian (''[[Heliconius charithonia]]'').<ref name="NABA"/><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Brown, Jr.|first=Keith|title=The Biology of Heliconius and Related Genera|journal=Annual Review of Entomology|year=1981|volume=26|pages=427–457|doi=10.1146/annurev.en.26.010181.002235}}</ref> It is a larval host plant for the glasswing butterfly (''[[Acraea andromacha]]'') in Australia.<ref>Braby, M.F., Butterflies of Australia; Their Identification, Biology and Distribution.  CSIRO Publishing 2000</ref>
